% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Figure: Cross-Model Heatmap (placed here for right-column [t] on p8)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\columnwidth]{figures/fig_crossmodel_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{DR reduction (\%) across 3 models $\times$ 2 datasets (zero-shot S1). Calibrated models (Qwen, Llama) achieve $\geq$90\% on SciERC; DocRED's higher $\bar{\kappa}$ reduces effectiveness. Full violation breakdown in Table~\ref{tab:cross-model} (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).}
\label{fig:crossmodel-heatmap}
\end{figure}

Neither layer alone suffices: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%, an enabling dependency that weakens at scale (84\% at 70B).
This non-additive interaction arises because the grammar layer provides a structured prerequisite: by restricting relation tokens to $\mathcal{R}$ and entity type tokens to $\mathcal{E}$, it ensures the semantic layer receives well-formed inputs on which domain/range lookups can operate.
Without grammar-enforced vocabulary membership, the semantic layer cannot reliably identify which relation governs a given type position.

OntoCoDec composes both layers, reducing DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% across model families and datasets ($\pm$0.3\,pp R-F1).
The residual DR$\to$CF conversion is a severity downgrade rather than an error introduction: DR violations produce ontology-invalid triples that corrupt downstream knowledge graphs and require re-extraction, while CF violations (cross-triple type inconsistency) preserve individually valid triples and are resolvable via beam search or post-hoc reranking.
Beam $k{=}4$ achieves near-zero violations at 8B, making generative IE reliably schema-compliant.

% Section 5 — Cross-Model Validation (compressed)
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_full_s1,
%          phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1,
%          llama_scierc_unconstrained, llama_scierc_full_s1,

\subsection{Cross-Model Validation}
\label{sec:cross-model}

S1 eliminates RV and ET for all models ($\leq$0.03\%); DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED (Figure~\ref{fig:crossmodel-heatmap}; Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}), with R-F1 improving in 5/6 settings.
Post-hoc filtering achieves DR${=}$0\% but at 15--74\% rejection rates (Appendix~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
\emph{Does grammar-constrained decoding alone resolve DR violations?}
Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} establishes that DR violations are pervasive (15--18\% across datasets) and that constraint layers interact non-additively: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%, the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}.
On DocRED (96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), grammar-only \emph{increases} DR via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: forcing out-of-vocabulary (OOV)$\to$valid relation mapping exposes violations previously masked by vocabulary errors (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:docred-zs-ablation}).
Cross-model validation (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}) confirms DR drops of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with R-F1 improving in 5/6 settings; post-hoc filtering achieves DR${=}$0\% but at 15--74\% rejection rates.
The DR-to-CF conversion is a severity downgrade, not an error introduction (Figure~\ref{fig:violation-composition}): DR violations produce ontology-invalid triples that corrupt downstream knowledge graphs and cannot be fixed without re-extraction, while CF (individually valid triples with cross-triple type inconsistency) can be resolved via fine-tuning, beam search, or post-hoc reranking (TCR eliminates all CF with bounded DR regression; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
Zero-shot evaluation thus establishes violation prevalence and constraint interaction; fine-tuning demonstrates practical elimination.

% Figure 6 (violation-composition) moved earlier in source for page 6 placement

% Cross-model table is in §6.1 (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning (expanded)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*
\emph{Does OntoCoDec retain value after fine-tuning?}
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 0.5--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}; full fine-tuning in Appendix~\ref{app:full-ft}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 (Bonferroni-corrected; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.69, {+}0.25]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).
Under fine-tuning, grammar becomes a no-op ($\Delta$DR$<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole DR defense (41--69\% on SciERC, 2--75\% on DocRED; Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}); three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR, all eliminated by S1 (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).
CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (63.3\%; Appendices~\ref{app:cf-distribution},~\ref{app:cascade-analysis}); beam ($k{=}4$) achieves near-zero violations at 8B (R-F1 43--46; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

% CF analysis folded into composability paragraph above; details in Appendices~\ref{app:cf-distribution},~\ref{app:cascade-analysis}.
% Table 2 (composability) moved to section5_crossmodel_draft.tex for page 8 placement

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (f) Downstream impact of DR elimination
%  exp_ids: task_e_lucky_violation_analysis
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Downstream impact.}
\label{sec:downstream-impact}
Constraint removal affects only 0.24\% of gold triples; error analysis confirms only 0.2\% of false negatives were blocked by constraints (Appendices~\ref{app:lucky-violations},~\ref{app:error-analysis},~\ref{app:case-studies}).
The 36 residual DR violations across fine-tuned settings decompose into entity type errors (39\%), schema gaps (33\%), and relation/direction errors (28\%); the irreducible floor is $\sim$3 violations (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

2	\label{app:related_work}
3	
4	% ===========================================================================
5	% Paradigm 1: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
6	% ===========================================================================
7	\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
8	Recent work has established efficient algorithms for restricting LLM outputs to conform to context-free grammars, making grammar-constrained decoding the de facto standard for obtaining structured output from language models.
9	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar} partitions the vocabulary into context-independent and context-dependent tokens and maintains persistent pushdown automata across decoding steps, achieving up to 100$\times$ speedup over prior CFG-constrained decoding methods.
10	Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines} reformulates constrained generation as finite-state machine transitions with offline vocabulary indexing, which enables efficient enforcement of regular-expression and JSON-schema constraints without runtime overhead per token.
11	LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql} introduces a declarative query language that compiles type, length, and regex constraints into token-level masks, providing a programmable interface for specifying multi-variable output structures.
12	These systems ensure that every generated token belongs to a grammar-valid continuation, but they do not address the \emph{distribution distortion} introduced by naive token masking.
13	A parallel line of work tackles this problem directly: DOMINO~\cite{beurer-kellner2024domino} minimizes distributional divergence during CFG enforcement by formulating mask selection as an optimization problem, and ASAp~\cite{park2024grammar} provides a provably unbiased sampling algorithm that preserves the original LM distribution under grammar constraints.
14	Together, these advances have made grammar-constrained decoding both fast and statistically principled, and provide a robust foundation for structured generation.
15	However, all of these methods operate exclusively at the syntactic level: they ensure format validity (e.g., well-formed JSON, valid enum values) but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints such as ontology domain/range rules that depend on previously generated content.
16	This syntactic-only limitation motivates OntoCoDec's semantic extension: our grammar layer builds on XGrammar for structural (JSON schema and enum) constraints, while a second semantic layer enforces relational type constraints that are inherently beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.
17	
18	% ===========================================================================
19	% Paradigm 1.5: Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code
20	% ===========================================================================
21	\paragraph{Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code.}
22	In programming-language generation, constrained decoding has been extended beyond syntax to enforce semantic properties such as type correctness; this work demonstrates that richer-than-CFG constraints can be compiled into token-level filtering.
23	In the text-to-SQL domain, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} maintains an incremental SQL parsing state that rejects tokens violating syntax or referencing non-existent database columns at each decoding step, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and CoSQL without modifying model weights.
24	While mechanistically similar to OntoCoDec's token-level filtering, PICARD operates over a \emph{fixed, fully enumerated} schema (database table and column names known before decoding begins).
25	In contrast, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated \emph{during} generation as entity spans are extracted from free text; constraint sets evolve with the decoding prefix, a fundamental distinction between querying a known schema and extracting from unstructured text.
26	Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} pioneers Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), which enforces syntax, type, and scope constraints simultaneously during code generation from pre-trained LMs without fine-tuning; this establishes that semantic constraints can be expressed as dynamic token masks conditioned on the generation prefix.
27	MGD~\cite{mgd_neurips2023} uses static-analysis monitors to perform incremental type checking at decode time; SantaCoder-1.1B with MGD outperforms text-davinci-003 on repository-level code completion by ensuring that every generated identifier is type-correct with respect to the surrounding code context.
28	Most recently, \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems, including generic types and subtyping, into prefix automata for token-level logits masking and reduce compilation errors by over 50\%.
29	This last system is the closest mechanistic analog to OntoCoDec, applying the same ``type system $\to$ automaton $\to$ logits mask'' pipeline, though in a fundamentally different domain.
30	The key technical difference lies in the constraint structure: programming-language type systems feature deep subtyping hierarchies and parametric polymorphism, whereas IE ontology axioms specify flat domain/range sets; a relation $R$ accepts head entities from set $\mathcal{D}(R)$ and tail entities from set $\mathcal{R}(R)$, with no subtype chains.
31	Conversely, IE introduces a challenge absent in code generation: the constraint target (entity type) must be inferred from free-text spans rather than read from declared type annotations, so a stateful entity registry must track extracted types during autoregressive generation.
32	These methods collectively demonstrate that semantic (type) constraints at decode time are both feasible and highly effective, but exclusively in the code domain where type systems are formally specified.
33	OntoCoDec is the first to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology axioms, including domain/range constraints, into token-level decoding masks for information extraction, migrating the type-constrained decoding paradigm from code generation to IE.
34	
35	% ===========================================================================
36	% Paradigm 2: Vocabulary/Type-Constrained Generation
37	% ===========================================================================
38	\paragraph{Vocabulary and Type-Constrained Generation.}
39	The idea of enforcing entity-type compatibility constraints for information extraction dates back to pre-neural methods.
40	\citet{roth_yih_2004} formulate joint entity and relation identification as an integer linear program (ILP) that enforces type constraints (e.g., \textsc{Emp-Org} only between \textsc{Per} and \textsc{Org} entities); this establishes the foundational principle that relational type compatibility should be a hard constraint, not a soft preference learned from data.
41	In the autoregressive era, GENRE~\cite{decao2021genre} pioneers trie-based constrained beam search for autoregressive entity retrieval, restricting each decoding step to tokens consistent with valid entity names from a predefined catalog.
42	GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie} extends this approach to end-to-end information extraction with state-based constraints that enforce valid triple structures, achieving strong performance on closed-world knowledge base population, though it requires task-specific fine-tuning on the target schema.
43	AdaKGC~\cite{adakgc_emnlp2023} introduces schema-constrained dynamic decoding with trie-based prefix trees that adapt to the target schema, enforcing that generated entity and relation names belong to a predefined inventory, a vocabulary-level constraint that ensures name validity but does not verify type compatibility between a relation and its arguments.
44	GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} provides a unified grammar-constrained decoding framework for structured NLP tasks including IE, introducing input-dependent grammars that adapt constraints based on the source text. GCD is the closest precursor to OntoCoDec in applying logits masking to IE, though limited to syntactic constraints.
45	NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} expresses lexical inclusion and exclusion constraints as predicate logic formulas enforced during beam search, offering a general mechanism for token-level control that can encode vocabulary membership but not relational type rules.
46	These approaches constrain \emph{which tokens} can appear (vocabulary membership) but not \emph{which type combinations} are valid for a given relation.
47	OntoCoDec's semantic layer enforces relational constraints (e.g., that the head entity of relation $R$ must belong to type set $\mathcal{D}(R)$) which cannot be expressed as static vocabulary restrictions because the valid set depends on the relation type generated earlier in the same sequence.
48	While Roth \& Yih's ILP formulation shares the same type-compatibility motivation, it operates as a post-hoc reranker over discrete candidates; OntoCoDec integrates enforcement directly into autoregressive decoding, preventing violations rather than filtering them.
49	
50	% ===========================================================================
51	% Paradigm 3: Structural Constraints for IE
52	% ===========================================================================
53	\paragraph{Structural Constraints via Training and Prompting.}
54	An orthogonal approach encodes IE output structure through model training or prompt design rather than decoding-time enforcement, relying on learned representations to produce schema-compliant outputs.
55	UIE~\cite{lu2022uie} defines a Structured Extraction Language and trains a unified text-to-structure model across 13 IE datasets, relying on large-scale pre-training to internalize output format constraints.
56	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} expresses annotation guidelines as Python dataclass definitions and fine-tunes Code-LLaMA to generate typed code, achieving strong zero-shot transfer to unseen IE schemas through the implicit type structure of programming languages.
57	KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} takes this further by encoding 29K entity types from Wikidata as a Python class hierarchy, training a Code-LLM to generate structured extraction code that implicitly respects type inheritance, the most comprehensive schema-as-code approach to date.
58	CodeIE~\cite{li2023codeie} similarly reformulates IE as code generation, using the structural regularity of programming languages to reduce output format errors.
59	ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie} uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align LLMs on IE tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source models while preserving general capabilities, though compliance with ontological constraints remains a learned soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
60	In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
61	These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining, precisely the ontology-portable scenario requiring no constraint-specific training that OntoCoDec targets.
62	EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} applies Answer Set Programming (ASP) constraints during decoding of joint entity-relation extraction models, enforcing structural type compatibility at generation time. This is a decoding-time approach, though

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information extraction (IE)~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations} (DR): structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations are pervasive (15--18\% of triples under zero-shot decoding and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning) and correlate with schema restrictiveness rather than model scale.
At competitive quality, even low residual violation rates compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendices~\ref{app:cross-model-zs},~\ref{app:posthoc-extended}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (CFGs) via XGrammar (JSON structure, vocabulary membership); the \emph{semantic layer} enforces type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to any autoregressive LM with logits access.
We validate across three model families, two RE datasets (up to 96 relation types), and event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}), with 70B-class supporting evidence (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
Composed with LoRA, greedy decoding reduces DR to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency), with 97.6--100\% of removed triples confirmed as false positives; beam ($k{=}4$) achieves near-zero violations at ${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency.
DR enforcement converts irrecoverable ontology violations into cross-field type inconsistencies (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned), a severity downgrade amenable to post-hoc resolution.

OntoCoDec is orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework that reduces domain/range violations to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) without retraining or significant quality loss, showing that these type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}).
    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only reduces DR by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, yet their composition achieves 94\%, because grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
    \item Supporting validation: scale-dependent interaction at 70B (semantic-only DR reduction grows from 24\% to 84\%; \S\ref{sec:70b-results}); beam $k{=}4$ achieves near-zero violations at 8B; event extraction generalization on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Figure: Cross-Model Heatmap (placed here for right-column [t] on p8)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\columnwidth]{figures/fig_crossmodel_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{DR reduction (\%) across 3 models $\times$ 2 datasets (zero-shot S1). Calibrated models (Qwen, Llama) achieve $\geq$90\% on SciERC; DocRED's higher $\bar{\kappa}$ reduces effectiveness. Full violation breakdown in Table~\ref{tab:cross-model} (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).}
\label{fig:crossmodel-heatmap}
\end{figure}

Neither layer alone suffices: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%, an enabling dependency that weakens at scale (84\% at 70B).
This non-additive interaction arises because the grammar layer provides a structured prerequisite: by restricting relation tokens to $\mathcal{R}$ and entity type tokens to $\mathcal{E}$, it ensures the semantic layer receives well-formed inputs on which domain/range lookups can operate.
Without grammar-enforced vocabulary membership, the semantic layer cannot reliably identify which relation governs a given type position.

OntoCoDec composes both layers, reducing DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% across model families and datasets ($\pm$0.3\,pp R-F1).
The residual DR$\to$CF conversion is a severity downgrade rather than an error introduction: DR violations produce ontology-invalid triples that corrupt downstream knowledge graphs and require re-extraction, while CF violations (cross-triple type inconsistency) preserve individually valid triples and are resolvable via beam search or post-hoc reranking.
Beam $k{=}4$ achieves near-zero violations at 8B, making generative IE reliably schema-compliant.

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
